newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia debt issuers take advantage of stability.
newsitem.headline: Australia debt issuers take advantage of stability.

text.p: The Australian non-government debt market saw a deluge of supply on Tuesday with A$1.0 billion of deals issued in a variety structures.

The timing of the supply was seen largely as coincidental, although market conditions are seen ripe for issuers as the debt market stabilises after the surprise 0.5 percentage point official interest rate cut to 5.5 percent on May 23.
The possibility of a further easing this cycle by the Reserve Bank, and subsequently lower funding costs, could also lure other borrowers into the market, analysts said.
Investors are also seen keen to take paper on board amid dwindling government and state government debt supply.

The three offerings announced Tuesday were a A$500 million four tranche securitisation deal for Macquarie Bank's PUMA, a A$300 million issue for St George Bank and a A$200 million offering from BTR Nylex.
The latter was the first corporate borrower rated A plus by Standard & Poor's to come to the market and was issued off its recently established A$500 million medium term note programme.

Peter Bloomfield, Senior Manager Debt Securities at Westpac, which jointly led the deal with Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said the programme was set up to provide BTR Nylex with the ability to diversify its funding base having previously sourced its funding through bank debt and domestic commercial paper.
The July 2000 dated deal will be priced at 37 to 41 basis points over the equivalent government bond on June 5.

"As this is the first corporate issue in the single-A part of the curve, bank issues are the only available benchmarks for pricing," said Jason Carley, Head of Research at ANZ Investment Bank in a research document.

"We would not expect a strong local corporate name such as BTR Nylex to trade more than five basis points over a foreign or regional bank. This gives a spread for BTR Nylex of 38 basis points over bond," Carley said comparing it to recent similar rated bank issues.
He added that it was well within many investors' authorised investment criteria and that a five basis point spread over bank issues was reasonable compensation for liquidity.
The shorter July 1999 St George issue was lead managed by BZW Australia and was priced at 36 basis points over government bonds to yield 6.215 percent.
An official for the lead manager said the issue was originally planned as a A$200 million offering.
The PUMA issue was its third for calendar 1997, taking total issuance for the year to date to over $1.9 billion, which includes its $912 million debut Euro issue launched in March.
The latest issue, to be known as PUMA Masterfund P-6, Series B, will be priced on or before June 6.
The largest tranche of the transaction is A$315 million of fixed coupon bonds due April 15, 2000. These are fungible with Masterfund P-6 Series A tranche 1-F and will carry a coupon of 6.9 percent.
The other tranches will be floating rate transactions.

"We expect to achieve competitive pricing on these bonds, based on PUMA's strong name in the marketplace, the fungibility of the fixed rate tranche and the structural enhancements built into PUMA issues," PUMA Managing Director Tony Gill said.
"These enhancements are designed to minimise some of the risk home by investors by providing investors with greater certainty over their cash flows," Gill added.
